points.t: Itchy wheals that **come and go within a day** ± lip or eyelid swelling; normal skin between.
Mast-cell histamine → dermal oedema (wheal) or deeper oedema (angioedema).
**Daily** second-generation H1 antihistamine, up-dose to 4× if needed; refer uncontrolled CSU.
**Anaphylaxis** → adrenaline / 999. ACE-inhibitor angioedema. Lesions > 24 h with bruising.

points: **Mast-cell degranulation**: IgE, autoimmune, idiopathic, or direct (NSAIDs, opioids, contrast).
**CSU** is usually **not** a food allergy: restrictive diets and patch tests don’t help.
**ACE inhibitors**: bradykinin angioedema, months to years after starting.
**Inducible**: dermographism, delayed pressure, cholinergic, cold, solar, aquagenic.

visuals.caption: Wheal (left): a mast cell releases histamine, small vessels leak and fluid lifts the upper dermis. Angioedema (right): the leak is deeper, in the lower dermis and fat, so the surface looks near-normal but the tissue swells.
visuals.alt: Skin sections comparing a urticarial wheal and angioedema

points: Itchy pink or skin-coloured wheals that **migrate** and leave normal skin.
**Acute** < 6 weeks; **chronic spontaneous** ≥ 6 weeks, most days.
**Angioedema**: lips, eyelids, hands, genitals; burns more than itches.
**Skin of colour**: feel for oedema when redness is subtle.
**Vasculitis clue**: > 24 h, burning or pain, purpura, residual bruise.

items.name: Dermographism
items.t: Linear wheals where skin is stroked.

items.name: Cold urticaria
items.t: Wheals on cold-exposed skin; warn about cold water.

items.name: Cholinergic
items.t: Small 2–5 mm wheals with flare on heat or exercise.

visuals.caption: Angioedema: deeper swelling of the lips and eyelids (also hands and genitals) that may burn more than itch. Skin colour is normal or slightly pink.
visuals.alt: Normal face beside the same face with swollen lips and eyelids

points: Timing of each wheal; phone photos.
Drugs: **ACE inhibitor**, NSAIDs, opioids.
**No routine tests.**
Keep minimal: FBC, CRP / ESR; thyroid only if indicated.
**Patch testing has no role.**
**UAS7 / UCT** for severity and omalizumab discussions.

cards.name: Contact eczema
cards.clue: Scaly, lasting days; patch testing relevant.

manage.lead: Take it every day, even on good days. Check BNF for dosing.

no.t: On an ACE inhibitor with swelling and no wheals?
no.sub: Stop the ACEI; emergency care if airway threatened

points: Remove triggers; avoid NSAIDs, aspirin, opioids if they aggravate; paracetamol preferred.
Cool measures; avoid overheating and tight clothes.

rx.dur: Every day in CSU, not as needed

points: Increase up to **4× licensed dose** (off-label); counsel sedation.
Switch agent if one fails at high dose. Sedating antihistamine at night only if sleep is wrecked.
Short oral prednisolone (up to 7 days per CKS) **plus** antihistamine. Avoid repeated courses in CSU.
Dermatology / allergy for **omalizumab** (NICE TA), then other immunosuppressants.
Montelukast sometimes on specialist advice; H2 blockers no longer routine.

limits.t: Stop the ACEI, don’t rechallenge; antihistamines and steroids help poorly. ARB only with caution and advice.

items.t: Lesions > 24 h with purpura: vasculitis work-up.
Fever, arthralgia, weight loss with urticarial rash: systemic disease / Schnitzler.

pearls.t: “It isn’t an allergy to something you keep eating”: most CSU is internal.
Daily dosing, even on good days; step down slowly.
Patch testing investigates eczema, not wheals.
Swelling without wheals on an ACE inhibitor: think bradykinin angioedema.

quiz.q: How long does an individual urticarial wheal last?
quiz.a: Less than 24 hours, leaving normal skin. Longer with bruising suggests urticarial vasculitis.

quiz.q: First-line treatment for CSU and how to take it?
quiz.a: A second-generation H1 antihistamine (cetirizine, loratadine or fexofenadine) every day, not as needed.

quiz.q: Next step if uncontrolled after 2–4 weeks?
quiz.a: Up-dose to up to four times the licensed dose (off-label), then refer for omalizumab if still uncontrolled.

quiz.q: Lip swelling without wheals on ramipril?
quiz.a: ACE-inhibitor (bradykinin) angioedema: stop the ACEI; emergency care if the airway is threatened.

quiz.q: Is patch testing useful in urticaria?
quiz.a: No: it investigates delayed contact eczema, not wheals.
